The wire capture separating "client never asked" from "server never sent" is the important part of this report — every other zero-usage issue I've seen stops at the symptom.

Worth adding to the fix design: whatever the transport, this bug shape has two failure surfaces at once. The DB rows are wrong (silent, discovered at invoice time) and the live session is wrong (user watches /bin/zsh.00 while burning tokens). A regression test that only asserts on the stored value can pass while the in-flight UI still lies, and vice versa — the captured request body asserting `stream_options.include_usage: true` is the stronger half of the pair, since it pins the contract rather than either consumer.

Also worth encoding: when `usage` is absent, the correct stored value is `null`/unknown, not `0`. Zero is a real measurement that can be summed and charted; unknown poisons every downstream average the moment it's conflated with a measured zero. Together's behavior here is lawful under the OpenAI spec (the field is optional without the flag), so the client owning the default is the right place for the fix

All four addressed in `8661d22fb1` (`fix(app): keep referenced chunks alive across live blob collection`).

**#1 and #2 — one mechanism.** Both are the same defect: live collection judged liveness by stored documents alone, while the renderer legitimately holds ids that no stored document references *yet* (an attachment uploaded before its 100 ms save window) or *any more* (a chunk republished on undo from the content cache). The fix is a grace period keyed on last reference:

- `blob.touched_at` (new migration `20260907031611_blob-touched`), set on `putBlob` and refreshed inside the same flush transaction for every blob a written document references — so a chunk republished from the renderer cache is refreshed even though no upload happened.
- Live collection removes only blobs that are unreferenced **and** untouched for `blobGrace` (15 min). Startup collection stays unconditional, since no renderer can hold an id then.
- The renderer reuses a cached chunk id without an upload for at most `draftChunkCacheTtl` (5 min) since its last use, and every use produces a document write that touches the blob within the write-behind delay. 5 min ≪ 15 min, so a cache hit can never publish a collected id. Past the ttl the chunk is uploaded again (`onConflictDoUpdate` on the host just refreshes `touched_at`).

Desktop tests: `collects a retired chunk only once it is unreferenced and past the grace period`, `a document that republishes a cached chunk id refreshes the chunk without an upload` (your undo sequence), `an uploaded attachment survives a due collection before its document is written` (your attachment sequence). App test: `a cached chunk id is uploaded again once it is older than the cache ttl`, which also clears the fake host's blobs in between and round-trips through a fresh store.

**#3 — surrogate pairs.** `split()` extends a piece by one code unit when it would otherwise end on a high surrogate. Test uses your `"x".repeat(draftTextChunk - 1) + "😀tail"` and asserts the round trip through the stored blob bytes and a fresh store, plus that the first piece is `draftTextChunk + 1` long.

**#4 — failed uploads.** A rejected `putBlob` promise is evicted from `chunkIds` (guarded so a newer entry for the same content is not removed), so the next save retries. `persisted()`'s draft write now also logs a rejected `setDocument` instead of leaving it unhandled. Test: `a failed chunk upload is retried on the next save instead of being reused`.

This issue might be a duplicate of existing issues. Please check:
- #47487: Agent accumulated 51 images via read tool, session bricked by provider 50-image count limit with no recovery — nearly identical scenario (read tool accumulating images, session stuck at the 50-image cap)
- #39677: Image-count 400s are not classified as context overflow, so media-strip compaction never triggers — same root cause (provider image limit not triggering compaction/recovery)

Both addressed in `6d080ab3ba` (`fix(app): repair blob references the store no longer holds on write`) — and you've convinced me the previous approach was the wrong shape. Timing-based protection (ttl vs grace) cannot be made sound while renderers hold ids the store can't see: the browser has no host process at all, and the composer keeps image ids in `savedHistory` indefinitely. So the guarantee now comes from **validation on write with repair**, independent of any collection schedule:

- `Driver.set(key, value)` returns the referenced blob ids the store does not hold. Desktop main answers with one SQL query over the (small, chunk-referencing) document — `json_tree` refs `NOT IN blob` — no JS parsing; the browser IndexedDB driver checks its `blobs` store.
- `setDocument` uploads the missing bytes again. During `encode` it records where each referenced blob's bytes can be produced: the chunk text itself, or the image `Blob` (kept alongside its object URL — `URL.createObjectURL` already pins it, so this costs no extra memory — with `fetch(url)` as the fallback). Ids are content hashes, so the queued document's reference becomes valid without a rewrite, and the write-behind flush that follows references the blob before any collection can run.
- The 5-minute cache ttl is **removed**: it was only a safety heuristic and it forced a re-upload of every chunk every five minutes. The desktop `touched_at`/`blobGrace` stays as an optimisation that keeps repairs rare (one cheap `UPDATE` per document flush).

Your two sequences are tests: `a cached chunk id the store no longer holds is uploaded again on the next save` (tab A/B: the driver's blobs are cleared between saves, undo republishes the cached id, a fresh store reads the text back) and `an image reference whose blob was collected is restored from its object url` (history image whose bytes were collected; the save republishes it and the bytes are back). Desktop: `set reports referenced blobs the store does not hold so the renderer can upload them again`.
Thanks for updating your PR! It now meets our contributing guidelines. :+1:

Both addressed in `257f94df44` (`fix(app): publish a repaired draft only after its blobs are restored`).

**#1 — publish after restore.** `Driver.set(key, value, strict)` now refuses a strict write while any referenced blob is missing and stores nothing, so the previously stored document stays visible to other windows. `setDocument` does a strict write first; in the common case that is the only round trip. When ids come back missing it uploads the bytes, then does a non-strict write of the repaired document. Test: `the previous document stays visible until missing blobs are restored` holds the repair upload on a gate and asserts the stored document is unchanged while it is pending.

**#2 — renamed ids.** `restore()` returns a map from the missing id to the id each upload actually came back with; `rename()` rewrites `blob.id` and `blob.ids` in the encoded document before the second write, and the chunk/image caches are updated under the new ids so the next save needs no repair. Test: `references are renamed when a restored blob comes back under a different id` uses a store that assigns fresh ids to every upload, and asserts the stored references changed, every referenced id is held, a fresh store reads the text and image back, and a subsequent save uploads nothing.

Anything still missing after restore has no bytes anywhere (an image reference whose blob was never loaded); it is published non-strictly and the owning codec drops it on read, as before. Desktop main honours `strict` (`set reports referenced blobs …` covers refuse vs. store), and the IPC payload gained the flag.

Both addressed in `e0ce800d32` (`fix(app): order browser draft writes and reuse restored image ids`).

**#1 — browser write ordering.** `createBrowserDraftStore().set` now runs the reference check and the document write in a single `readwrite` transaction over `["blobs", "documents"]`. The `put` is issued from the last `getKey` success callback (never from a promise continuation), so the transaction is never left without a pending request and cannot auto-commit early. IndexedDB serialises overlapping readwrite transactions in creation order, so a later small save or `removeItem()` (also readwrite on `documents`) is ordered *after* this one and can no longer be overtaken by the older write. The desktop path was already ordered (one synchronous IPC handler). I couldn't add an automated test for this — the repo has no IndexedDB in the Bun test environment and no `fake-indexeddb` dependency — so this one rests on the transaction model; your IndexedDB reproduction is the check.

**#2 — restored image ids.** `restore()` records `aliases: old → new` when an image comes back under a different id (re-pointing any earlier chain so lookups stay one step), and `encode` resolves a live reference's id through it before publishing and before looking up its bytes. The existing random-id test now continues with three cursor-only saves of the still-live reference and asserts the published image id stays the restored one and nothing is uploaded.

> ## Plugin permission assertions
> 
> - Add plugin-only `ctx.permission.assert(input)` to Effect and Promise plugins, using the existing permission engine.
> - Check canonical browser URLs before dispatching tab operations.
> - Check server-file reads and external-directory access before sending upload bytes to the desktop.
> - Check a captured network request's URL before returning its details to the agent.
> - Preserve permission decisions, feedback, and cancellation without a new HTTP endpoint or permission engine.
> 
> ```ts
> yield* ctx.permission.assert({
>   sessionID: tool.sessionID,
>   agent: tool.agent,
>   action: "browser",
>   resources: [url],
>   source: { type: "tool", messageID: tool.messageID, id: tool.id },
> })
> ```
> 
> ```mermaid
> flowchart LR
>   Tool[Plugin tool] --> Rules[Existing permission engine]
>   Rules -->|allow| Operation
>   Rules -->|ask| Approval[Existing approval UI]
>   Approval --> Rules
>   Rules -->|deny| Refusal
> ```
> 
> These are action and disclosure checks, not a firewall for every browser subresource or redirect.
> 
> Final layer after the plugin (#46531) and desktop implementation (#44838).
>

### Follow-up with hard evidence: the Go usage counter does not match real usage

Since opening this, the Go dashboard (opencode.ai/go) shows **monthly usage at 50 % (~30 $ / 60 $)**, while 5 h and weekly both sit at 0 %. Given the state of my account during this window, this is impossible — and it's the clearest proof that the fault is server-side, not on my side.

**What actually happened** (from `opencode.db`, opencode's own `session.cost`):

| Date   | Go messages | Recorded Go cost |
|--------|-------------|------------------|
| 09-02  | 235         | 0.63 $           |
| 09-03  | 49          | 0.13 $           |
| 09-04  | 47          | 0.05 $           |
| 09-05  | 573         | **3.59 $** (the one productive day) |
| 09-06  | 147         | 0.99 $           |
| 09-07  | 26          | 0.05 $           |

- **Total recorded Go spend: ~5.43 $** (≈ 9 % of the 60 $ monthly allowance) — not 30 $.
- On **09-06** (the day the 429s started) there are **10 sessions with a recorded cost of 0.00 $** (empty, blocked attempts).
- The log contains **319 HTTP 429** responses and **277 "rate limit exceeded"** entries, all on `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/messages`, each returning a `retryAfterMs` of ~42,000,000 ms (~12 h) that keeps resetting.

**Conclusion:** a counter reporting ~30 $ of consumption for a window in which I was receiving 429s most of the time — while the free Zen models worked instantly in parallel — can only be a server-side metering/billing error. The usage shown as billed but never actually delivered must not be charged to my account.

**Updated request:**
1. Correct the Go usage meter — the ~30 $ / 50 % shown is not attributable to real, delivered usage.
2. Compensate the ~3 days of unusable service (as originally requested) — an extension/credit, and reverse any usage recorded during the blocked window.

Logs/timestamps and the `opencode.db` aggregate available on request; happy to share the exact log excerpts privately (billing-related).

Je corrige mon commentaire précédent pour être **strictement exact** (en contentieux, une valeur gonflée n'aide pas) :

Le chiffre « 319 HTTP 429 » que j'ai donné incluait aussi les 429 du **endpoint Zen gratuit** (`opencode.ai/zen/v1/chat/completions`) et du **provider Mistral**. 

**Comptage précis, endpoint Go uniquement** (`https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/messages`) :

| Mesure | Valeur |
|--------|--------|
| Réponses HTTP 429 sur le endpoint Go | **39** |
| Marqueurs `retryAfterMs` sur le endpoint Go | **44** |
| `retryAfterMs` observés | 37 626 000 → 48 533 000 ms (~10,5 h → 13,5 h) |

Le point clé reste inchangé et est même **renforcé** : les 429 sont bien **spécifiques au endpoint Go** (les modèles Zen gratuits répondaient instantanément en parallèle), et le compteur mensuel affiche **50 % (~30 $)** alors que le coût enregistré localement (`session.cost`) n'est que de **~5,47 $** sur la même fenêtre.

### Full evidence bundle — for cross-checking against server-side data

Here is everything needed to compare with your own server-side records. All figures are reproducible from the files below.

**Environment:** opencode 1.18.29 · CachyOS (Arch) · xfce4-terminal · account `laurentm28`.

---

**1. Recorded spend per day** — from `opencode.db`, opencode's own `session.cost` field, provider `opencode-go`:

| Date       | Recorded cost ($) |
|------------|-------------------|
| 2026-09-02 | 0.63              |
| 2026-09-03 | 0.13              |
| 2026-09-04 | 0.05              |
| 2026-09-05 | 3.59              |
| 2026-09-06 | 0.99              |
| 2026-09-07 | 0.14              |
| **Total**  | **5.53**          |

Query: `SELECT date(time_created/1000,'unixepoch'), round(SUM(cost),4) FROM session WHERE json_extract(model,'$.providerID')='opencode-go' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;`

---

**2. HTTP 429 on the Go endpoint** — `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/messages`:

- **Date range of 429s on the Go endpoint:** from `2026-09-05T20:24:11Z` through `2026-09-06`.
- **40** `retryAfterMs` markers on **2026-09-06**, ranging **37 626 000 → 51 105 000 ms** (~10.4 h → 14.2 h), re-arming each time.
- Log line format:
  ```
  timestamp=2026-09-06T13:32:54.809Z ... url=https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/messages method=POST status=429 attempt=1 ... retryAfterMs=37626000
  timestamp=2026-09-06T13:33:55.106Z level=WARN ... url=https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/messages method=POST status=429
  ```
- Counts: `grep -a "status=429" "$LOG" | grep -c "zen/go/v1/messages"` and `grep -a "retryAfterMs" "$LOG" | grep "zen/go" | grep -c "2026-09-06"`.

---

**3. Blocked (no-output) sessions on 2026-09-06** — **10** sessions with recorded cost **0.00 $**:
`SELECT count(*) FROM session WHERE json_extract(model,'$.providerID')='opencode-go' AND cost=0 AND date(time_created/1000,'unixepoch')='2026-09-06';`

---

**4. Token volumes** (why the bill diverges) — GO assistant messages, all time:
- cache **read**: **72.58 M** tokens
- cache **write**: 2.33 M
- input: 1.55 M · output: 0.57 M

The cache-read volume is the dominant cost driver in these agentic sessions. If your server-side meter prices cache reads differently from the local `session.cost` estimate, that explains a large part of the gap between the dashboard figure and the recorded spend.

---

**5. Dashboard reading (2026-09-07 06:42 CEST)** — screenshot saved locally:
- 5 h: **0 %** · Weekly: **0 %** · Monthly: **50 % (~30 $ / 60 $)**, reset in 25 d 13 h.

Given the recorded spend above is **5.53 $** over the same window, a **50 % monthly** reading (~30 $) does not match the locally recorded usage. Please compare this against your own metering records.

---

Ran into this on Windows. In my case the timeout was caused by a port collision with Windows dynamic port reservations. On Windows, especially with Hyper-V, WSL2 or Docker installed it likes to reserve large blocks of ports.

The CLI hung and eventually threw:
- Error: Timed out waiting for the background service to start

Checking `~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log` showed the actual error:
- Managed service port 49374 on 127.0.0.1 is already in use by another process.

Running `netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp` confirmed that Hyper-V/WSL had reserved ports
49336 to 49435, preventing the background service from binding to 49374.

Setting an unreserved port resolved it: ```powershell opencode service set port 40900 opencode service start```

Two improvements would probably help here:
1. Surface stderr from the background service in the CLI rather than silently waiting for the timeout.
2. Retry with an alternate port (or request port 0 and persist what the OS assigns) when hitting EADDRINUSE / WSAEACCES.

Cross-platform confirmation with a tightly isolated repro, via `opencode serve` 1.18.27 (npm, Linux), driven by the Paseo orchestrator (0.7.2).

**Setup:** 6 MCP servers in global `opencode.json` (5 local stdio incl. three Google servers spawned from the *same* python script with different args: `gmail`, `gdrive`, `gcalendar`; plus one remote with OAuth). All six report `{"status": "connected"}` from `GET /mcp` for the entire run; zero `MCP connection closed` log lines during the observed window; the local servers verified working by direct stdio JSON-RPC `tools/list` + `tools/call`.

**Symptom:** long-lived sessions permanently lose a *subset* of MCP tools. Two sibling sessions in the same serve process, same directory, same project/instance, same agent (`build`), same model+variant (litellm/kimi-k3, reasoningEffort=max):
- session created 07:24 → permanently missing `gmail_*` (15) + `gcalendar_*` (9) for its whole lifetime, while `gdrive_*`, `gitlab_*`, `fathom_*` work fine.
- sessions created later (08:11 via raw HTTP API, 08:37 via Paseo) → full tool set including all `gmail_*`/`gcalendar_*`.
An earlier session (06:35) was missing only `gcalendar_*` while using `gmail_*` successfully — i.e. the frozen subset differs per session, matching a cache snapshotted at session/instance bring-up and never invalidated, as described in #40015 (here reproduced server-side, not Desktop).

**Ruled out:** provider/gateway trimming (fresh sessions get all 24 google tools through the same LiteLLM gateway, verified by the model enumerating and calling them; requests up to ~75k tokens unaffected), model variant, agent config, and the orchestrator payload (it passes no `tools`/`system` overrides).

**Workaround:** create a new session — full tool set returns. Affected sessions never recover.

This cluster (#33027, #40015, #16491, #26357) really looks like one root cause: `MCP.tools()` serves connect-time cached defs (`s.defs`), and a session/instance snapshot of "available tools" is never recomputed when that cache changes. A `ToolsChanged`-driven invalidation (or per-prompt recompute) would fix all of them.

## Confirmed on Windows 11 + Japanese IME with opencode2 (V2 beta) — byte-level evidence and a working workaround

### Environment

- `opencode2 v0.0.0-beta-19215` (`@opencode-ai/cli` from npm)
- Windows 11, Japanese MS-IME
- Windows Terminal (classic conhost behaves the same)
- TUI

### Symptom

While the Japanese IME is active (hiragana mode):

- `ctrl+x` (leader) is recognized — the pending indicator appears in the footer
- the follow-up key (`m`, `l`, ...) never triggers the combo: the committed character is inserted into the prompt as text (fullwidth `ｍ`), and the next Enter submits the prompt — so it *feels* like "pressing m sent my draft"
- direct `ctrl` bindings (`ctrl+p`, `ctrl+o`, ...) keep working, because control keys bypass the IME

The default keybind table in this build matches the docs, and no user config overrides it — this is not a configuration problem.

### Root cause (verified with a raw stdin dump)

With `ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT` (the same input mode the TUI uses), the bytes delivered per key press are:

| Key | IME off (direct input) | IME on (hiragana) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a` | `61` | `e3 81 82` (あ) |
| `ctrl+x` | `18` | `18` |
| `m` | `6d` | `ef bd 8d` (FULLWIDTH ｍ, U+FF4D) |
| `ctrl+alt+k` | `1b 0b` | `1b 0b` |
| `ctrl+p` | `10` | `10` |

With the IME on, plain letter keys arrive as **committed UTF-8 text, not key events**, so the leader follow-up key never matches `<leader>m` / `<leader>l` / etc. Unlike the desktop/web `isComposing` case, the Windows console has no composition event at all — the console just delivers committed text.

I also verified this end-to-end with an automated ConPTY (winpty) harness: injecting `18` followed by `6d` opens the model dialog, while injecting `18` followed by `ef bd 8d` inserts `ｍ` into the prompt. Same result with `--standalone` and the shared background service, on two beta builds (`beta-19213`, `beta-19215`), in both Windows Terminal and conhost.

### Workaround (works today)

Rebinding the frequent commands to `ctrl`/`alt` combos — which bypass the IME — in `~/.config/opencode/cli.json` keeps them usable with the IME on:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/v2/cli.json",
  "keybinds": {
    "model.list": "<leader>m,ctrl+l,alt+m",
    "session.list": "<leader>l,ctrl+y,alt+l",
    "session.new": "<leader>n,alt+n",
    "agent.list": "<leader>a,alt+o",
    "opencode.status": "<leader>s,alt+s",
    "theme.switch": "<leader>t,alt+t",
    "messages.copy": "<leader>y,alt+y",
    "session.undo": "<leader>u,alt+u",
    "session.redo": "<leader>r,alt+r",
    "session.compact": "<leader>c,alt+c",
    "session.sidebar.toggle": "<leader>b,alt+v"
  }
}
```

Verified in the same harness: `ctrl+l`, `alt+m`, `ctrl+y`, `alt+l`, `alt+o`, `alt+s`, `alt+t` all trigger their commands while the IME is active. Keeping the `<leader>` alternative preserves the old behavior when the IME is off.

Note: the korean-keymap plugin approach from #21163 does **not** help on this path. I built a Japanese version of it — `keymap.appendEventMatchResolver` installs and runs, but IME-committed characters are routed to the editor as text and never reach keybind matching.

### Related

- #8652, #13805, #16252, #21163 — same class on other IMEs/platforms
- PRs #6753 (physical `baseCode` matching) and #20888 (`isComposing` guards) were closed unmerged. One extra note for this case: on the Windows console the terminal delivers legacy VT encoding (verified above), so `baseCode`-based matching alone would not fix it — committed text characters need to be considered as key events (e.g. normalizing fullwidth → ASCII for keybind lookup), or the leader pending state needs an IME-aware design.
